{{short description|Austronesian language spoken in the Solomon Islands}} {{Distinguish|text = the [[Huave language]] of Mexico}}{{Parenthetical referencing|date=April 2026}}{{Infobox language | name = Hoava | states = [[Solomon Islands]] | region = Marovo Lagoon (Nggerasi Lagoon), [[New Georgia Island]] | speakers = 460 | date = 1999 | ref = e18 | familycolor = Austronesian | fam2 = [[Malayo-Polynesian languages|Malayo-Polynesian]] | fam3 = [[Oceanic languages|Oceanic]] | fam4 = [[Northwest Solomonic languages|Northwest Solomonic]] | fam5 = New Georgia – Ysabel | fam6 = [[New Georgia languages|New Georgia]] | iso3 = hoa | glotto = hoav1238 | glottorefname = Hoava | map = Lang Status 80-VU.svg | mapcaption = {{center|Hoava is classified as Vulnerable by the [[UNESCO]] ''[[Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger]]''.}} | dia1 = Hoava | dia2 = [[Kusaghe dialect|Kusaghe]] | dia3 = Njela | lc1 = ksg | ld1 = Kusaghe }} '''Hoava''' is an [[Oceanic languages|Oceanic language]] spoken by 1000–1500 people on [[New Georgia Island]], [[Solomon Islands]]. Speakers of Hoava are multilingual and usually also speak [[Roviana language|Roviana]], [[Marovo language|Marovo]], [[Pijin|Solomon Islands Pijin]], English.{{clarify|all of the above or only some?|date=February 2023}} == Dialects == Hoava has a distinct dialect, [[Kusaghe dialect|Kusaghe]].{{Sfn|Davis|2003}} == History == Hoava is an [[Austronesian languages|Austronesian]] language that is spoken mostly on the island of [[New Georgia]]. New Georgia is a mountainous island, 85 kilometres long and 41 kilometres wide at its widest part, with a total area of {{convert|2,145|km2|mi2}}, covered with dense rainforests. {{Sfn|Davis|2003}}The island was involved in a series of World War II battles, later named the [[New Georgia Campaign]], which lasted from June 20 to November 3, 1943.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}} == Population == Hoava is spoken in three known locations: [[Western Province (Solomon Islands)|Western Province]], New Georgia Island, and [[North Marovo lagoon]], but mainly New Georgia Island. According to a 1986 census there are about 2,360 speakers of the language, but as of the 1999 census, the language is spoken by 460 people, suggesting a huge decline in the number of speakers. == Endangerment == ===Materials=== There are not many materials written in Hoava. The only material of outside world access is a guide to grammar by Karen Davis and a storybook, which is only beginning to fall out of use. There are translations of the Bible and stories but not much else is known about surviving materials. ===Vitality=== According to ''[[Ethnologue]]'', Hoava has a 6b (Yellow) endangerment status. "Intergenerational transmission is in the process of being broken, but the childbearing generation can still use the language so it is possible that revitalization efforts could restore transmission of the language in the home" (Lewis 2013). Without intergenerational transfer, main outlet uses will soon be destroyed or fade away while other languages take its place. With the decrease of L1 speakers, the value of the language in the community will only drop until it is no longer applicable to the community. Combined with the low number of speakers, if no action is to take place, Hoava will fade to away into disuse. ==Phonology== ===Consonants=== Hoava uses 16 consonants in its [[phoneme]] system, {{IPA|/p, t, b, d, s, β, m, n, r, l, dʒ, k, g, ɣ, ŋ, h/}}. {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |+ ! colspan="2" | ![[Bilabial consonant|Bilabial]] ![[Postalveolar consonant|(Post)]] [[Alveolar consonant|alv]] ![[Velar consonant|Velar]] ![[Glottal consonant|Glottal]] |- ! rowspan="2" |[[Plosive]] ![[voiceless]] |p |t |k | |- ![[voiced]] |b |d |g | |- ! colspan="2" |[[Nasal consonant|Nasal]] |m |n |ŋ | |- ! colspan="2" |[[Fricative]] |β |s |ɣ |h |- ! colspan="2" |[[Affricate]] | |ʤ | | |- ! colspan="2" |[[Approximant]] | |l | | |- ! colspan="2" |[[Trill consonant|Trill]] | |r | | |} ===Vowels === Hoava uses five vowels: {{IPA|/i, ɛ, a, ɔ, u/}}. There is no [[phonemic distinction]] of vowel length, although vowels can be lengthened when stressed.{{Sfn|Davis|2003}} The vowels can be combined into pairs with the weight of two syllables.{{Sfn|Davis|2003}} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |+ ! ![[Front vowel|Front]] ![[Back vowel|Back]] |- ![[High vowel|High]] |i |u |- ![[Mid vowel|Mid]] |ɛ |ɔ |- ![[Low vowel|Low]] |a | |} ===Syllable structure=== Hoava has an [[open syllable structure]] of (C)V. Two vowels occurring together are counted as two syllables, since they function as such for transitive marking rules.{{Sfn|Davis|2003}} For many Oceanic languages of the [[Austronesian languages|Austronesian]] family group it is common that words do not end in consonants. ==Morphology== ===Reduplication=== [[Reduplication]] is frequently used in Hoava as a method of word formation, to express intensification, and to form the progressive aspect of a verb. Reduplication is used to create words denoting entities related to the referent of the source word, either as part of the entity, or having a resemblance to it, or being a metaphorical extension". * {{lang|hoa|bui}} 'lost'; {{lang|hoa|bu-bui}} 'forgot' * {{lang|hoa|yasa}} 'jump'; {{lang|hoa|yasa-yasa}} 'jumping' === Pronouns === ==== Personal pronouns ==== Information in the following sections is based on Davis 2003:45-109,{{harvnb|Davis|2003|pages=45–109}} unless otherwise stated. Subsequent references give only relevant page numbers and figures. In Hoava there exist three sets of characteristics in order to distinguish which [[personal pronoun]] is to be used. This includes whether the pronoun is first, second or third person; the plurality needed; whether it is singular or plural and whether it is inclusive or exclusive. {| class="wikitable" |+Personal pronouns
(pg. 46, Figure 63) |- ! colspan="2" | ! Singular ! Plural |- ! rowspan="2" | 1st person ! {{small|exclusive}} | rowspan="2" | {{lang|hoa|rao}} | {{lang|hoa|gami}} |- ! {{small|inclusive}} | {{lang|hoa|gita}} |- ! colspan="2" | 2nd person | {{lang|hoa|goe}} | {{lang|hoa|gamu}} |- ! colspan="2" | 3rd person | {{lang|hoa|i(sa)}} | {{lang|hoa|ria}} |} There are a number of extra circumstances and exceptions which are also present when discussing the use of personal pronouns. One specific example of this is the third-person singular form {{lang|hoa|isa}}, which is used as an emphatic (forcible) form or used to refer to a particular topic. Speakers of Hoava tend to use {{lang|hoa|sa}} for a more general pronoun. The third-person pronoun {{lang|hoa|eri}} is used with a dual form created by using the number 'two' {{lang|hoa|karu}} after a plural pronoun. A trial form is also created by using the number 'three' prefix {{lang|hoa|ka-hike}}. The dual forms are obligatory whereas trial forms can be replaced by a simple plural. Forms specific for four people are common when it is significant to know that four people were involved. The number 'four' follows the pronoun with the number prefix added, e.g. {{lang|hoa|gita ka-made, gami ka-made}}. Other numbers can be substituted into a sentence in the same matter. When these dual or numerical forms are used, it is most commonly at the start of a narrative to add the names of the others in the group. This does not include the speaker themselves. These pronoun forms can come before a noun phrase in [[apposition]]. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Sagele pule mae eri karu.|go.up return come PRO:3PL two|'They (two) came back up.' (Pg 47, Figure 68) }} Some other characteristics to note with the use of pronouns in Hoava are that pronouns can be followed by [[demonstrative]]s and by the restrictive particle {{lang|hoa|qa}}; an example of this can be seen below. There exist some cases in Hoava in which it is not completely necessary for a pronoun to be present or where exceptions to the use of pronouns exist. Firstly, it is common for the pronoun to be dropped from a sentence completely once it has been made clear who is being referred to, or if it is clear who is being referred to by other information such as object markers. Also, the dropping of pronouns referring to animate objects is predominantly done with first-person singular and plural and second-person plural pronouns in object position, as the object marker on the verb is the same as the pronoun. Inanimate objects in Hoava do not often have a [[Pronoun|pronominal]] reference, a construction which resembles a pronoun to identify the object. However, it is possible to use a pronoun for an inanimate object even though it is rare. In Hoava there exist no [[Reflexive pronoun|reflexive]] forms of the pronouns. In order to create the same meaning as a reflexive, the verb {{lang|hoa|pule}} (meaning 'return') is used. "There is no subject or object pronoun used, other than the object marker on the applicative suffix...in any of the sentences elicited with the pule used in this manner." (pg.49) {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Vaquru teqe pule-ni-rao qa.|new cut return-AP-1SG REST|'I've just cut myself.' (Pg 49, Figure 78b) }} As seen in the example above, {{lang|hoa|pule}} has been used with the applicable [[suffix]] and the singular exclusive first-person pronoun {{lang|hoa|rao}} to create the meaning of the reflexive form 'I've'. Also, the pronoun is followed by the restrictive particle {{lang|hoa|qa}}, which is a characteristic that was mentioned earlier to sometimes occur with the use of pronouns. The morpheme {{lang|hoa|tale-}} can also be used in the instances mentioned above, but rather than performing a reflexive function, it acts as an emphasis that no other people were involved apart from the speaker. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Vaquru teqe pule-ni-a tale-na.|new cut return-AP-3SG alone-3SG|'(She) has just cut herself.' (Pg. 49, Figure 79) }} Within the [[lexicon]] of Hoava there are some verbs which have an inherent reflexive meaning built in and therefore the use of an extra form which suggests that it is reflexive is not needed. These are verbs which automatically mean performing an action to oneself, such as {{lang|hoa|hele}} 'wash oneself' or {{lang|hoa|viraka}} 'scratch (oneself)'. ==== Demonstrative pronouns ==== In Hoava there exists a three-way spatial differentiation of [[deixis]]. This includes proximal, close to the speaker; distal, close to the hearer; and remote, distant for the speaker and the hearer. Of the three sets of demonstratives in Hoava, two sets concern the use of pronouns: a set of long forms that are used as both noun modifiers and as demonstrative pronouns and another set which is restricted to being used only as demonstrative pronouns. An extra set of 'near to hearer' long demonstratives is also used both as a noun modifier and demonstrative pronoun. These sets all have both singular and plural forms which can be used. {| class="wikitable" |+Long demonstratives

An example of the use of long demonstratives is as follows: {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Heri''' ria nikana vihe.|'''PROX:PL''' ART:PL man choose|'These are the chosen men.' (pg.85, figure 204d) }} It is more common in Hoava for the [[morpheme]]s {{lang|hoa|isana}} and {{lang|hoa|tiara}} to be used in place as demonstrative pronouns in favour of the singular distal demonstratives {{lang|hoa|sani}} and the plural {{lang|hoa|sari}}. It is also not common for the remote demonstratives {{lang|hoa|Huani}} and {{lang|hoa|Huari}} to be used. Hoava has a set of short demonstratives, which are a group of particles found after the noun head of a noun phrase. They have the noun-modifying function of adding a sense of definiteness and they may also signify tense. They can be used with common nouns, names, and pronouns. {| class="wikitable" |+Short demonstratives

Figure 264 a and c) }} === Person marking === Hoava has two optional articles, {{lang|hoa|E}} and {{lang|hoa|se}}, which may or may not be used with personal names or personified animals and birds. These articles are used before the name and although {{lang|hoa|Se}} is more likely to be used over {{lang|hoa|E}}, neither example is completely necessary and can be dropped. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|{Samu Gobe} misianare tami gami|{Samu Gobe} teacher POSS:1PL.EX PRO:1PL.EX|'Our teacher was Samu Gobe.' (Pg. 59, Figure114b) }} == Negation == Hoava has four types of sentential negation; {{lang|hoa|kipu}}, {{lang|hoa|kae}}, {{lang|hoa|kahi}} and {{lang|hoa|maki}}. All of these negative particles are placed before the predicate. === The negator {{lang|hoa|kipu}} === The negator {{lang|hoa|kipu}} expresses factual negation, whereby the speaker claims that what they are saying is correct. As shown below, {{lang|hoa|kipu}} can be used in past and present events. These are asserted to be factual. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Kipu''' gilalí rao vivine-di ria ra.|'''NEG''' know.TR:3PL PRO:1SG story-3PL PRO:3PL DEM|'I don't know the stories of them.' }} {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Saonae '''kipu''' pule sa loa-na.|long.time '''NEG''' return ART.SG spouse-3SG|'Her husband did not return for a long time.' }} {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Kipu''' isa qa sa pakupaku.|'''NEG''' PRO:3SG REST ART:SG necklace|'It's not the necklace.' (Pg. 243, Figure 68a, b and c) }} However, {{lang|hoa|kipu}} can also be used to indicate future events that are expected to be true. Note that {{lang|hoa|kipu}} can both precede and follow the future particle. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Pula ve, koni '''kipu''' ta-va-mate.|if like FUT '''NEG''' PASS-CAUS-be.dead|'If so, (he) will not be killed.' }} {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Kipu''' koni tavetí ria ba sara.|'''NEG''' FUT make.TR:3PL PRO:3PL EMPH those|'They will not make ''those''.' (Pg. 243, Figure 69a and b) }} Below, {{lang|hoa|kipu}} is placed after the definite article of a nominal predicate: {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Se Matakale sagi na '''kipu''' tu-na sa nikana so.|ART M. TOP ART '''NEG''' child-3SG ART:SG man PAST:SG|'Matakale, he was not a son of man.' (Pg. 243, Figure 70) }} In cases where a noun phrase is placed before the verb phrase or noun phrase predicate, {{lang|hoa|kipu}} is not fronted. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Ria pa Vareso, ria '''kipu''' ṉaní sa.|PRO:3PL PRP V. PRO:3PL '''NEG''' eat.TR:3PL PRO:3SG|'Those from Vareso, them he did not eat.' (Pg. 243, Figure 71) }} {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Na koburu isana '''kipu''' tiqu-a hinaquru.|ART child that '''NEG''' tough-TR:3SG girl|'That child, girls didn't touch him.' (Pg. 243, Figure 72) }} {{lang|hoa|Kipu}} can also be found within imperative clauses: {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Veko-a, '''kipu''' ilisoqo-a.|leave-TR:3SG '''NEG''' hurt-TR:3SG|'Leave him, don't hurt him.' (Pg. 243, Figure 73) }} === The negator {{lang|hoa|kae}} === The negator {{lang|hoa|kae}} is occasionally shortened in Kusaghe to {{lang|hoa|ke}}. It is used to emphasise events and states that are not possible, not allowed or which run counter to the usual state of affairs. {{lang|hoa|Kae}} is used to mark events and states that are not possible due to some factor which prevents their occurrence. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Isa sa pu '''kae''' dugili-ni-a Pilipi.|PRO-3SG PRO:3SG REL '''NEG''' be.deaf-AP-3SG Pilipi|'That's what stops Pilipi from being deaf.' (Pg. 244, Figure 74a) }} Prohibitions can also use {{lang|hoa|kae}}. Similar to {{lang|hoa|kipu}} which can be used with imperatives, {{lang|hoa|kae}} can also be used to display everyday imperatives which are generally used towards children. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Kae''' kabo.|'''NEG''' cry|'Don't cry.' }} {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Kae''' do{{=}}dola la-ia ṉina goe se Maqiqo na.|'''NEG''' REDUP{{=}}stare go-TR:3SG possibly PRO:2SG ART Mangginggo DEM|'Don't you go staring at that Mangginggo.' (Pg. 244, Figure 76a and b) }} Another use of {{lang|hoa|kae}} is when an event of state is not the expected one, such as an event that was expected to happen but did not. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Kae''' atu velu ba rao so.|'''NEG''' go.to.you yesterday EMPH PRO:1SG PAST:SG|'I did not come to you yesterday.' (Pg. 245, Figure 78) }} {{lang|hoa|Kae}} can also be used for hypothetical events that are not generally expected to occur. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Pula vena '''kae''' ta-poka labete, doluru kasitoṉa heri, koni uke qa sa kabasa.|if SIM '''NEG''' PASS-be.nailed board all thing these FUT fall REST ART:SG house|'If boards, all these things, are not nailed, the house will fall.' (Pg. 245, Figure 80a) }} Contradictory statements is often expressed using the phrase {{lang|hoa|kae gua}}, which means 'not so, not as stated'. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|“Vegoa, solodia goe ni?” gua isa. “Kari, solodia '''kae''' gua.”|how soldier PRO:2SG DEM said PRO:3SG no soldier '''NEG''' said|'“What, are you a soldier?” he said. “No, (I'm) not a soldier.”' (Pg. 246, Figure 82a) }} === The negator {{lang|hoa|kahi}} === {{lang|hoa|Kahi}} which means 'not yet' is a negator used to express the likelihood that an event or state will occur, despite not having taken place yet at the point in time referred to. {{lang|hoa|Kahi}}, like the other negative particles, can be seen to precede the verb phrase. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|Kipu hana ṉani pu '''kahi''' varavara, mi varavara paki tu tiqe ṉani qa.|NEG anyhow bite COND '''not.yet''' pray but pray first REST then bite REST|'(You) don't eat if have not yet prayed, but pray first and then eat.' (Pg. 247, Figure 84a) }} === The modal negator {{lang|hoa|maki}} === {{lang|hoa|Maki}} is a modal negative particle which expresses the desire of the speaker that negative consequences of an event do not occur. It is placed immediately before the verb phrase. {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Maki''' ta-ṉani leboto.|'''{{gcl|NEG:WARN|negative modal}}''' PASS-bite machete|'Don't be hurt by the machete.' }} {{interlinear | lang = hoa | indent = 3|'''Maki''' uke goe.|'''{{gcl|NEG:WARN|negative modal}}''' fall PRO:2SG|'Don't you fall.' (Pg. 247, Figure 85) }} == Syntax == ===Basic word order=== In traditional typology Hoava is a [[verb–subject–object]] (VSO) language. There are some modifications to this particular pattern for focusing and [[topicalization]] purposes.{{Sfn|Davis|2003}} ==Vocabulary== ===Indigenous vocabulary=== * {{lang|hoa|hore}} 'canoe' * {{lang|hoa|leboto}} 'bushknife' * {{lang|hoa|igana}} 'fish' * {{lang|hoa|inebara}} 'feast' * {{lang|hoa|pirae}} 'now' * {{lang|hoa|tavete}} 'make' * {{lang|hoa|keke}} 'one' * {{lang|hoa|mae}} 'come' * {{lang|hoa|toka}} 'follow' * {{lang|hoa|puta}} 'sleep' * {{lang|hoa|gua}} 'did' * {{lang|hoa|heleana}} 'river' * {{lang|hoa|ko}} 'be' * {{lang|hoa|tala}} 'where' * {{lang|hoa|la}} 'go' * {{lang|hoa|koburu}} 'child' * {{lang|hoa|ome}} 'see' === Numerals === Hoava has a [[Decimal|decimal system]] of numbering.{{Sfn|Davis|2003}} # {{lang|hoa|keke}} 'one' # {{lang|hoa|karua}} 'two' # {{lang|hoa|hike}} 'three' # {{lang|hoa|made}} 'four' # {{lang|hoa|lima}} 'five' # {{lang|hoa|onomo}} 'six' # {{lang|hoa|zuapa}} 'seven' # {{lang|hoa|vesu}} 'eight' # {{lang|hoa|sia}} 'nine' # {{lang|hoa|manege}} 'ten' == References == {{Reflist}} * {{Cite book |title=A Grammar of the Hoava language, Western Solomons |last=Davis |first=Karen |date=2003 |publisher=Pacific Linguistics |isbn=978-0-85883-502-3 |series=Pacific Linguistics 535 |location=Canberra |doi=10.15144/PL-535 |hdl=1885/146158 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free }}
